To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 1780–1793 dome-building eruption of Mount Hood, Oregon triggered the formation of a sediment wave in headwater can-yons of the Sandy and Salmon River, that the wave was subsequently flushed downstream by lahars and flood flows, and that the resulting sedimentation in the lowermost 87 km of the Sandy River raised the channel bed at least 23m and resulted in the formation of 11 new terraces.
the Sandy River experienced channel aggradation and subsequent degradation in response to sedimentation from a dome-building eruption that began in A.D.

the magnitude and rate of channel aggradation, and the timing of the transition to degradation, in response to a moderate-volume dome-building eruption at a low-latitude, mid-latitude volcano in the Cascade Range, Oregon, were similar to those of other rivers subjected to very large inputs of volcaniclastic sediment, and were likely enhanced by the lateral confinement of the river in an incised valley.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the magnitude, rate, and timing of channel aggradation and the recovery of a river following heavy sediment loading.
the response of a large, unconfined, low-gradient, alluvial river to a very large, but relatively modest, sediment input from a volcanic source.
the timing and magnitude of channel response to a dome-collapse eruption at Mount Hood and the role of lahars and seasonal flooding in the sedimentation and channel response in the Sandy river.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the magnitude of channel response to sediment loading and the timing of channel recovery in the Sandy and other rivers are strongly dependent upon local factors that control the magnitude and timing of sediment delivery to the depositional zone.
the magnitude of channel response to sediment loading is not necessarily related to the magnitude of volcanic eruption, the intensity of rainfall, or the volume of sediment delivered to a river.

the Sandy River channel aggraded at least 23–30 m in a few decades in response to sediment input during the 1780–1793 eruption of Mount Hood, and then degraded over a period of at least half a century to a new equilibrium state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a combination of a very large volume of coarse sediment delivered to a sediment reservoir, a confined channel with a steep gradient, and a climate dominated by frequent moderate to high-intensity rainfall events, all of which were present at Mount Hood, can result in channel aggradation that approaches that resulting from large explosive eruption in other volcanic environments and rainfall regimes.

the Sandy River experienced an extreme aggradation event in response to a moderate-volume eruption, and that the resulting channel response and recovery were comparable to those of rivers elsewhere that have been subjected to much larger sediment loads from explosive eruptions.
a dome-building eruption of a volcano in a humid, moderate-rainfall climate can produce a sediment load capable of aggrading a downstream river channel by several tens of meters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Sandy River provides a case study of a channel response to a relatively modest dome-building eruption that was more extreme than the response to many larger eruptions at other volcanoes.

the magnitude of channel response to heavy sediment loading is strongly controlled by local conditions, including the magnitude of the sediment input, the rate of delivery, and the channel’s response to the imposed load.

the magnitude of channel response to sediment loading is strongly influenced by the magnitude of sediment input and by local factors, such as valley confinement, that influence sediment delivery and transport.
